extracted.intended_audience: general readers; aspiring working-class youth and readers of Andrew Carnegie's autobiography
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting practical life-and-career principles and behavioral criteria implied in an autobiographical chapter (Andrew Carnegie) about youth, work, and self-improvement. Focus is on the explicit and implicit criteria the author presents for advancement and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal public education / parental duty to educate children
rubrics_metrics.description: Scotland was the first country that required all parents, high or low, to educate their children, and established the parish public schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as context/example (Aaleck, Jock, and Jeanettie 'are up and got their lair' — footnote 'Education'). Suggests public schooling as foundational to opportunity and social improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance / never give up
rubrics_metrics.description: Of one thing I was sure, he ought never to give up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie repeatedly emphasizes persistence: enduring unpleasant work, concealing troubles as a matter of honor, and believing 'something will come' if one keeps on. Perseverance is presented as a primary virtue leading to opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seize opportunities promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a great mistake not to seize the opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated when Carnegie volunteers 'I could stay now if wanted' for the telegraph post despite doubts; immediate willingness to accept a chance leads directly to appointment and advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start at the bottom and work upward
rubrics_metrics.description: We all began at the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: sweeping offices, bathing spools in oil, running a steam-engine in a cellar. The narrative frames beginning low as normal and a foundation for promotion (e.g., messenger → clerk → operator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue self-improvement via education
rubrics_metrics.description: We all determined to attend night school during the winter and learn the larger system [double-entry bookkeeping].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions: attend night school, read widely (Macaulay, Bancroft), use Colonel Anderson's library. Education is both formal (night school) and informal (public library, theater) and directly tied to career mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice skills whenever possible / hands-on learning
rubrics_metrics.description: We had an opportunity of practicing upon the telegraph instruments before the operators arrived ... I soon began to play with the key ... I succeeded in getting the message and ran out with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie learned telegraphy by practicing while sweeping and by taking messages by ear; practical, opportunistic practice is shown as a path to competence and promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperate financially / pool small earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: I proposed that we should 'pool' these messages and divide the cash equally at the end of each week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pooling 'dime messages' solved quarrels among boys and taught early lessons in financial organization and fair sharing—presented as a positive anti-conflict practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master local knowledge and people
rubrics_metrics.description: I therefore began to note the signs of these houses ... Before long I could shut my eyes and, beginning at the foot of a business street, call off the names of the firms in proper order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorizing business names/locations and knowing employees saves time and confers advantage as a messenger; local knowledge is a practical competence for job performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate relationships with prominent people
rubrics_metrics.description: My position as messenger boy soon made me acquainted with the few leading men of the city ... many a telegraph message [delivered to them].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being noticed by and acquainted with influential figures (judges, businessmen) provides role models and tangible benefits (compliments, opportunities). Networking is framed as a route to advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial discipline and family budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Every penny that I could save I knew was needed at home ... a silver half-dollar ... hid until two hundred were gathered, when I obtained a draft to repay the twenty pounds ... The Carnegie family was free from debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful saving, transparency in household finances (mother as treasurer), and debt repayment are shown as sources of security and pride; discipline in small finances matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of public libraries and access to books
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonel James Anderson announced that he would open his library of four hundred volumes to boys ... The fundamental advantage of a library is that it gives nothing for nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to books (Colonel Anderson's library) is credited with opening 'treasures of literature' and being transformative for working boys; Carnegie later founds libraries on this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to small matters because trifles can be pivotal
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon such trifles do the most momentous consequences hang.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chance conversation over a game of draughts led to the inquiry that resulted in Carnegie's messenger position. The author cautions that small acts/words/looks can determine large outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiative and resourcefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: I was appointed treasurer [of the pooled dimes] ... I shut off the paper slip, took pencil and paper and began taking the message by ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking practical initiatives—proposing systems, assuming responsibilities, improvising to take a message—earns trust, responsibility, and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate wholesome influences and avoid low fellowship
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing contributed so much to keep my companions and myself clear of low fellowship and bad habits as the beneficence of the good Colonel [Anderson].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to books and respectable company is presented as a preventative against vice and a supportive influence for moral and intellectual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cultural exposure (theater, music) to broaden taste and language
rubrics_metrics.description: The theater ... stimulated my love for Shakespeare ... Wagner was revealed to me in 'Lohengrin' ... the rhythm and the melody ... seemed to find a resting-place in me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attendance at theater and musical performances broadened literary and musical appreciation and aided memory and expressive ability; cultural experiences are framed as educational and character-forming.
